## 20.222 *** THE DUMP PAID OFF: 20.209 R2 IS WRONG - THE ENTITY RECEIVE CHAIN IS **NOT**
## *** STATICALLY UNREACHABLE. THE HANDLER TABLE IS IN .rdata AND ALWAYS WAS; THE SCAN
## *** LOOKED FOR THE WRONG POINTER FORM. ent_recv = obj[+0xA8]->slot[10].
## *** (2026-08-31 16:5x, VERIFIED-BY-READING, no boot)

### RESULT 1 - THE CORRECTION, AND WHY IT WENT UNSEEN FOR A WEEK
20.209 R2 scanned the image for qword pointers equal to 0x141718510 (ent_recv's IMAGE-based
VA) and found ZERO, concluding "nothing calls, jumps to, or takes the address of the entity
receive entry ... dispatched exclusively through a runtime-built table". That conclusion
drove 20.209 R4's "which carrier is right CANNOT be named statically" and, through it, the
parking of the whole carrier question.
IT IS WRONG. destiny2_unpacked_full.exe is a DUMPED image: its .rdata holds RUNTIME-RELOCATED
pointers (base 0x7FF6AF7F0000 baked in), not image-based ones. The pointer to ent_recv is
stored as 0x00007FF6B0F08510. A scan for 0x141718510 could never have matched.
RULE (new, and it generalises): in THIS image, a qword pointer scan must search for
`runtime = 0x7FF6AF7F0000 + rva`, not for the static VA. Every "zero pointer references"
null in the corpus that was produced by a static-VA qword scan is now SUSPECT.

### RESULT 2 - HOW IT WAS FOUND (the dump doing the job it was taken for)
p2-146 dump (rig, both clients in Tower). RE_scripts/dump_search.py (new, registered in
TOOLS.md) scanned all 1,703 committed ranges / 6.49 GB for the runtime address
0x7FF758418510 (rig base 0x7FF756D00000 + rva 0x1718510): EXACTLY ONE hit, at
base+0x1C9AE28. 0x1C9AE28 is inside .rdata, which is fully raw-backed - so the same
pointer was in the file all along, and reading the static image at 0x141C9AE28 confirmed it.
The dump named the address; the static image then confirmed and extended it, at no boot cost.
ORACLE: dump_search --selftest found "player_broadcast" at base+0x1CA1518, matching 20.209
R3's independently recorded static VA 0x141CA1518 exactly - the scan and the base
conversion are both verified against a known-good address.
ent_header 0x141717EB0 and ent_create 0x141718080: ZERO runtime pointers. Consistent with
20.209/20.210 - they are reached by direct CALL from ent_recv, not dispatched.

### RESULT 3 - THE STRUCTURE: A 73-ENTRY TABLE OF FOUR 15-POINTER HANDLER BLOCKS
Table 0x141C9AD90..0x141C9AFD0, 73 entries, 8-byte stride. ent_recv is entry #19.
Marker 0x141A31340 recurs at 17/32/47/62 - PERIOD 15. Four blocks, and the slot two past
each marker holds a DIFFERENT sibling: 0x141718510 (ent_recv), 0x141718AE0, 0x1417183C0,
0x141718CB0 - four implementations of the same receive slot, one per record type.
Rip-relative refs into the table (full-width scan of BOTH .text sections; note xref_scan.py
returned 0 on an address whose reference was already read by hand this session, so it was
not used - see TOOL DEBT): blocks are taken at 0x141C9ADD8 (#9), 0x141C9AE50 (#24),
0x141C9AEC8 (#39), 0x141C9AF40 (#54), plus the table base 0x141C9AD90.

### RESULT 4 - THE INSTALLER NAMES THE DISPATCH SHAPE
0x1416CACD0 (1777 B) installs all four blocks into ONE object:
    [rsi+0x1680] = 0x141C9AF40   [rsi+0x140] = 0x141C9AEC8
    [rsi+0x100]  = 0x141C9AE50   [rsi+0xA8]  = 0x141C9ADD8   <- ent_recv's block
ent_recv's block sits at [obj+0xA8], and ent_recv is slot 10 within it (entry 19 - entry 9).
SO: ent_recv is reached as **obj[+0xA8]->vtbl[10]**, i.e. `call qword [reg+0x50]` after a
load of [obj+0xA8]. It is a VIRTUAL METHOD ON A SUB-OBJECT, not a message-type table entry.
CONSEQUENCE for the carrier question: the carrier is not selected by a wire type indexing a
table - it is selected by WHICH OBJECT the caller holds. The next question is therefore
"who calls through [+0xA8] slot 10", which is a searchable code pattern, not a guess.

### RESULT 5 - WHY NO CARRIER WAS BUILT THIS SESSION (deliberate)
The user asked for the gameplay-plane carrier built "exhaustively empirically accurate".
It could not be: the gameplay-plane hypothesis rests on ONE volume observation (20.209 R4 -
the largest flow in the p2(136) pcap was rig<->server:30976 at 118 KB), which identifies no
protocol, no message type and no framing; and the fork's server/gameplay/ subsystem has
essentially no message-type space to extend (one constant, kRecordType = 6). Building it
would have required inventing an opcode, an envelope and slot addressing - three
placeholder fields, which is the p2(133)/p2(134) failure class and is exactly what 20.209 R4
warned against in writing. NOT BUILT, ON PURPOSE. The work above is what makes it buildable.

### TOOL DEBT (both real, both cost time this session)
- xref_scan.py returned "0 refs" for 0x1427E45D0 while a rip-relative reference to it at
  0x140B47D22 had already been read by hand minutes earlier. Its nulls are not trustworthy;

- TOOLS.md describes rig_dll_helper.py as "remote-thread memory reads on the rig client";

## 20.223 *** THE RECEIVER IS NOT INSTANTIATED. NO OBJECT IN 6.49 GB HOLDS THE ENTITY-
## *** RECEIVE VTABLE. ent_recv's ZERO CALLS ARE NOT "NOTHING SENT IT A MESSAGE" - THERE
## *** IS NOTHING TO SEND TO. NO CARRIER COULD HAVE WORKED.
## *** (2026-08-31 17:1x, VERIFIED-BY-READING + VERIFIED-BY-DUMP, no boot)

### RESULT 1 - THE RUN AT 0x141C9AD90 IS A VTABLE GROUP, NOT A MESSAGE TABLE
20.222 called it a "73-entry handler table". Refined: it is a C++ multiple-inheritance
vtable group. 0x1416CACD0 stores four of its interior addresses into ONE object:
    [obj+0xA8] = 0x141C9ADD8   [obj+0x100] = 0x141C9AE50
    [obj+0x140] = 0x141C9AEC8  [obj+0x1680] = 0x141C9AF40
which is the secondary-vptr layout of a class implementing four interfaces. ent_recv
(table entry 19) is SLOT 10 of the secondary vtable at 0x141C9ADD8, i.e. reached as
`obj[+0xA8]->vtbl[10]`, equivalently `call qword [reg+0x50]` after loading [obj+0xA8].

### RESULT 2 - THE DISPATCH IS VIRTUALISED (clean .text cannot answer it)
Full-width scan of BOTH .text sections for `mov r64,[reg+0xA8]` ... `call qword [reg+0x50]`
within an 80-byte window: ZERO hits in the first .text; 2 hits, both inside the SECOND
.text (0x1454D06F4, 0x146ECD8CD) - the virtualised region. So the call site is protected
and is not recoverable by reading clean code.

### RESULT 3 *** THE DECIDING MEASUREMENT: NO INSTANCE EXISTS ***
p2-146 dump (rig, both clients in Tower, players valid 0x3, loop actively rejecting the
peer). Searching all 1,703 ranges / 6.49 GB for each secondary vtable at its rig runtime
address (base 0x7FF756D00000):
    0x7FF75899ADD8 (#9, ent_recv's) .... 0 hits
    0x7FF75899AE50 (#24) ............... 0 hits
    0x7FF75899AEC8 (#39) ............... 0 hits
    0x7FF75899AF40 (#54) ............... 0 hits
    0x7FF75899AD90 (primary) ........... 1 hit, heap object 0x233461F1D90
That single object carries the PRIMARY vptr at +0 and a second vptr at +0x40 - and its
+0xA8 is ALL ZEROS (read directly: 0x233461F1E38 .. +0x40 = 00). So not one object in the
process has the entity-receive interface installed.
CONCLUSION: the receiver object is NEVER CONSTRUCTED in a live two-player Tower session.
ent_recv's zero calls across every boot are not "the carrier never sent it anything" -
THERE IS NO RECEIVER TO SEND TO. 20.210 R3 and 20.213 R2 retired the cluster for the wrong
reasons; 20.222's un-retirement stands, but the reason is different again and stronger.
*** THIS IS WHY NO CARRIER WAS BUILT (20.222 R5). A wire message to an uninstantiated
receiver cannot work, so building one would have been wasted regardless of framing. ***

### RESULT 4 - WHAT 0x1416CACD0 ACTUALLY IS: NOT YET ESTABLISHED (open, labelled)
20.222 R4 called it "the installer". Its four callers are 0x1416FFD60, 0x1416FFE00,
0x141702580, 0x141709B10 (all in the entity-manager neighbourhood; the last is ~0x300 B
from the lifecycle driver 0x141709800 of 20.220). But the call site at 0x141709D96 is a
TEARDOWN path - it zeroes [r14+rsi*8+0x178], decrements [r14+0x170], calls 0x1416E9CF0,
then calls 0x1416CACD0. In C++ BOTH constructors and destructors install vtables, so
whether 0x1416CACD0 constructs, destructs, or is one of a ctor/dtor pair is UNRESOLVED.
Do not build on "installer" until this is read. The other three call sites are unread.

### RESULT 5 - THE FRONT
Not "which carrier reaches ent_recv" (unanswerable and premature) but:
WHAT CONSTRUCTS THE ENTITY-RECEIVE OBJECT, AND WHY DOES IT NOT HAPPEN HERE?
Next, in order, all offline: (1) classify 0x1416CACD0 ctor vs dtor by reading its head and
its other three call sites; (2) if a ctor exists elsewhere, find its gate; (3) the dump can
then confirm whether the gate's inputs are present. femu --graft-dump is available for

Every result in R3 is offline, repeatable, and cost no boot. This is the Tier-1/Tier-2

## 20.224 *** THE CONSTRUCTOR IS FOUND AND THE WHOLE CONSTRUCTION CHAIN IS NAMED.
## *** THE ENTITY-RECEIVE OBJECT IS BUILT PER-INDEX INTO A 31-SLOT REGISTRY, AND THE
## *** ACTIVITY-KIND==5 ANSWER IS A **PARAMETER**, NOT A GATE. (2026-08-31 17:3x,
## *** VERIFIED-BY-READING + VERIFIED-BY-DUMP, no boot)

### RESULT 1 - CTOR vs DTOR, SETTLED (20.223 R4 discharged)
CONSTRUCTOR = 0x1416BB1E0 (leaf, no unwind data; a `ret` at 0x1416BB1DF precedes it, and
it touches only rcx/rax/rdx). It installs the four secondary vptrs AND initialises members:
  [rcx+0xA8]=0x141C9ADD8  [rcx+0xF0]=0xFFFFFFFF  [rcx+0xB0]=0  [rcx+0x100]=0x141C9AE50
  [rcx+0x108]=0  [rcx+0x140]=0x141C9AEC8  32x `mov byte [rdx],0` at +0x29C stride 0xA0
  [rcx+0x150]=0  [rcx+0x1680]=0x141C9AF40  [rcx+0x1688]=0  [rcx+0x16BC]=-1
  [rcx+0x16A8..0x16C8]=0
Field init to -1 and zeroing a 32-entry array is construction, not destruction.
TEARDOWN = 0x1416CACD0 (opens with the obfuscator's encrypted-global pattern; sets only

### RESULT 2 - THE REAL GATE CHAIN (0x141702611..0x141702675), FOUR CONDITIONS
Per participant `ebp`, all with r14 = the PARTICIPANT ARRAY base:
  1. ebp = 0x1404DF480(r14)         first set bit of the presence bitmask [r14+0x5924C];
                                     -1 -> bail entirely

0x2AC0-byte per-participant records - the same stride 0x1404DF620 uses (20.226 context).

The disp8 write scan written for +0x44 has NO instruction-boundary validation - it matches
the byte pattern anywhere, including mid-instruction. It reported 0x1416F43F6 as

0x14171812A) were confirmed by disassembling at the reported address. ANY future disp8
scan must disassemble-to-confirm before a hit is cited. field_xref.py remains disp32-only,
which is why the scan existed at all - generalising field_xref to disp8 WITH boundary
validation is the right fix rather than keeping a scratch scanner.

    +0x5924C  read by 0x1404DF480 -> first set bit = the participant index (cond 1)

    2. i != self index (0x1403CB2F0)
    3. bit i of [table+0x59248] SET

    5. bit 4 of byte[ table + i*0x2AC0 + 0x38 ] SET (0x1404DD470 true) -> CONSTRUCT

### RESULT 2 - THREE ANCHORS TRIED, THREE TOOL LIMITS (all nulls are INSTRUMENT nulls)

     (0x846C8338F7D022E6 / 0xF5D3535B98AEB768) and tested every cross pair for a delta

     (`lea rax,[rcx+0x59000]; mov [rax+0x24C],edx`) matches neither half. ENCODEDS

## 20.232 *** THE maskA DISCREPANCY IS EXPLAINED (SELF IS FOUND BY IDENTITY, NOT INDEX),

### RESULT 1 - HOW "SELF" IS IDENTIFIED (and why i=0's FAIL-cond3 may be a non-event)
Gate condition 2 compares the participant index against 0x1403CB2F0(r12), a thunk:
`mov rdx,rcx; add rcx,8; jmp 0x1404DD640`. So self index = 0x1404DD640(r14, r12), which:
    r9d = [table+0x5924C]                    ; maskB
    walk its set bits from 0; for each i:
      rax = [table + i*0x2AC0 + 8]           ; a QWORD at record+8
      cmp rax, [r11]                         ; r11 = r12 = table_obj+0x6C30
      je  -> this i is SELF
      else advance to the next set bit
SELF IS FOUND BY IDENTITY MATCH ON record+8, not by a fixed index. CONSEQUENCE for
20.230 R2: i=0's FAIL-cond3-maskA-bit-clear may simply be self being excluded from maskA -
in which case it is correct behaviour and NOT a discrepancy. The p2-148 probe does not
evaluate cond 2, so its per-participant verdict cannot currently distinguish "self, rightly
skipped" from "peer, wrongly rejected". A future probe should log the self index alongside.
UNRESOLVED against that reading: SOLO, maskA was 0x1 with maskB 0x1 - i.e. the single
participant WAS in maskA. If that participant was self, "maskA excludes self" is false.
Both readings survive the current data; the self index would settle it in one line.

So under every encoding field_xref covers, no participant-record +0x38 writer exists in

## 20.233 *** THE 0x2AC0-STRIDE SCAN: 59 SITES IMAGE-WIDE, EXACTLY ONE IN THE POOL
## *** CLUSTER - A PARTICIPANT-TABLE INITIALIZER THAT DOES **NOT** TOUCH +0x2C OR +0x38.
## *** (2026-08-31 20:0x, VERIFIED-BY-READING, no boot)

### RESULT 1 - THE SCAN (surgical; the naive form was killed twice for hanging)
Method that worked: byte-prefilter .text for the imm32 0x00002AC0 (bytes c0 2a 00 00) - a
SUPERSET, so nothing is missed - then disassemble only at the hits. 59 sites total (58 in
.text#1, 1 in .text#2). The naive form (capstone over all 113,818 .pdata functions) and a
bash loop spawning pdata_bounds per address both had to be killed; neither would have
finished. Prefilter-then-decode is the pattern for any future constant hunt.

### RESULT 2 - WHERE THE 59 SITES ARE
  0x1404DD1EB / DD476 / DD676 / DF4E9 / DF506 / DF609 / DF626 ... the gate predicates
      (0x1404DD470's read and 0x1404DD640's self-index walk among them) - already known
  0x1404F72DF ................ THE ONLY POOL-CLUSTER SITE (see RESULT 3)
  0x140726169..0x140726389 ... 33 sites at regular ~0x11 intervals: a table or unrolled
      sequence, NOT a constructor. Do not chase it as one.
  ~14 scattered singles (0x140C18E43, 0x140E2278C, 0x1411D78FB, 0x14123F80D, 0x1416F0C94,
      0x1419142BF, 0x144FBF63E ...) - unexamined, each is a single indexing site.

### RESULT 3 - THE POOL-CLUSTER SITE IS A TABLE INITIALIZER, AND IT SKIPS BOTH GATE FIELDS
fn 0x1404F7240 (chained; body 0x1404F7270..0x1404F7469, 505 B), in the pool cluster beside
the pool ctor 0x1404F77D0. Its loop walks records by the 0x2AC0 stride:
    mov dword [rax-0x10], 0x811C9DC5     ; FNV-1a 32-bit offset basis - a hash seed
    mov dword [rax],      r12d
    mov dword [rax+0xB0], 0x811C9DC5
    lea rax, [rax+0x2AC0]                ; next record
then a second loop over [rbp+0x55BA0] with stride 0xE8, and `mov [rsp+0x40], 0x59260` -
note 0x59260, adjacent to the gate masks at 0x59248/4C/50.
IT WRITES -0x10, +0x00 AND +0xB0. IT DOES NOT WRITE +0x2C (identity) OR +0x38 (the gate
byte). So the record CONSTRUCTOR does not initialise the gate bit - consistent with
p2-148's 904/904 readings of 0x00, and it means bit 4 of +0x38 must be set later, by
something outside every encoding field_xref covers (20.232 R2).

### RESULT 4 - AN ATTRIBUTION ARTIFACT, CAUGHT
The first pass reported "fn 0x1405B9260 with 33 stride sites" as the likely record
constructor. FALSE: 0x1405B9260's .pdata entry spans 4,341,096 bytes - a catch-all range,
not a function. Any .pdata attribution should sanity-check the range size before the
enclosing function is named. The 33 sites are the 0x1407261xx run above.

### RESULT 5 - WHAT THIS DOES TO BLOCKER 3
Combined with the other session's dispatcher decode (all 21 handled activity-message types
checked; none writes the gate bitmasks or +0x38), and with 20.232 R2 (no writer in any
covered encoding), the feeders are now cornered into: client-internal derivation, a

excluded. That is a real narrowing, and it raises the odds that the eventual fix is a
CLIENT-SIDE WRITE rather than a server wire field - which changes what "behavioural
change" means for this lane (see the handoff).

(member+0xED/+0xEF, peer+0xD0 bit 10) which the fork publishes as ZERO, so even with
c4=1 the evaluator may mark nothing" - is WRONG, by disassembly of 0x140C171F0:
  0x140C1744D shr eax,0xA / and al,1 -> je +6 -> `mov byte [rbx-5],1`
  0x140C1745D call 0x14177A080 -> test al,al -> je +6 -> `mov byte [rbx-4],1`
  0x140C1746F call 0x14177A060 -> test al,al -> je +6 -> `mov byte [rbx-3],1`
None of the three branches skips the entry; each only writes an informational byte
into the per-entry descriptor (rbx, stride 0x18, array at rbp+0x290). The ONLY hard
conditions are the present-mask bit, state != 3, state == 0xA (both live-satisfied
per lane K) and then `call 0x1404F7680 / test al,al / je` = THE c4 BYTE. c4 is the
last input, not one of several. The activation block that follows writes
`dword [rbx+4] = 5` + the latch - and state-5-vs-0 is the same asymmetry the
20.236/20.237 dumps recorded for the peer record. p2-154's expected effect is
therefore SHARPER than the sketch claimed.

### RESULT 4 - THE CONTACTABLE BYTE NEVER MOVED (the boot's answer: NO)
track_c4 (the +0x602C4 reader 0x1404F7680) is a RETWATCH probe: emit_retwatch calls
probe_changed() and emits on EVERY change of the masked byte, with NO call budget (the
`12` in its probe row bounds only the enter/leave pairs). It therefore cannot miss a
0 -> 1 transition anywhere in the session.
  mac: ONE retwatch line, `call=1 al=0 raw=0x0`, across 39,790 calls.
  rig: ONE retwatch line, `call=1 al=0 raw=0x0`, across 29,058 calls.
No second line on either machine. The byte was 0 at the first read and never anything
else. `bit4=1` appears ZERO times in the mac's whole pgate stream.

EXONERATED (do not re-litigate these):

    returned al=1 and set pool+0x602C4 = 1; a wrong-id body left it 0

  - THE TRANSPORT/FRAMING. The body reached both clients and was accepted.
  - THE ROW. It exists, keyed by exactly the machine id the body carries.
REFUTED: chain mark L5 of BOOT_BRIEF_p2-154, which was marked ASSUMED and named as
"THE BOOT'S REAL RISK": *type 45 routes to handler 0x1404F3870 on the live client*.
It does not - or it routes and the handler takes a live path femu's dump-backed run did
not. Those two are NOT yet separated (see R6). What is certain is that the byte the
handler exists to write did not get written.

### RESULT 6 - THE DISCRIMINATOR (the next instrument, one boot, client-side)
The inference "the handler never ran" is NOT yet evidence - U13 applies to my own
reading here as much as anywhere. Hook, in one build:
  (a) 0x1404F3870 itself (the type-45 handler) - does it fire at all?
  (b) 0x1404F7DF0 (the pool dispatcher lane I mapped) - does the message reach dispatch?
  (c) the handler's flag-gate branch at 0x1404F3934 - femu took the gate-FAILED path and
      still wrote; if live takes the other branch the record-build runs instead
      (0x1403055A0/0x140305140/0x140372A60), code femu never executed.
Outcomes: dispatcher fires + handler does not = a registration/route gap (consistent
with 20.241 R4: pool handlers arrive via a RUNTIME registration-table callback, so a
type can be accepted at the message layer and have no registered consumer). Neither

and the body needs a pool envelope rather than an outer svc9 type - which would also
mean type 30's success (p2-144) reached the pool by a route we have mis-generalised.

### RESULT 2 - WHY p2-154 SAW NOTHING (both causes named, neither is the encoding)
 (a) TIMING: mac call=3 (t=295547) hit the pool with rows=1 - only the mac's own row; the
     peer's row was created 2 ms later (trackadd t=295549). A body one tick early marks
     nothing, exactly as designed. Only call=4 (t=300607, 5 s later) found rows=2.
 (b) POOL TARGETING: on the MAC the first two type-45 bodies dispatched to a DIFFERENT
     pool object - pooldisp t=196093 pool=0x1D367480, and poolc4 shows that object with

     The rig never had this split (pooldisp t=57922 pool=0x27D214EF988, the same object as
     everything else). So a client can hold more than one pool object and a body can land
     on the one with no tracking rows. The recurring push is what rescued it: a later body
     hit the right pool.

It reaches the dispatcher (type 45 is table entry 16 -> 0x1404F3870, confirmed live) and
the handler runs - 4 calls on the mac, 2 on the rig.

### RESULT 3 - AND IT CHANGED NOTHING (the boot's real finding)
 - THE READER STILL RETURNS 0. track_c4 (0x1404F7680) is change-gated with no budget, so
   any 0->1 it observed would emit. It emitted ONCE per machine, al=0 (mac:1987 t=165220,
   rig:1733 t=57922), and never again - while still being called (mac census 7,167 calls
   and climbing at t=379292). So the reader is being asked about a row/pool whose byte is
   still 0, NOT the row we set. Each client's OWN row (r0) is c4=0x00 throughout; only the
   PEER row (r1) is 1. The likeliest reading, UNPROVEN: the evaluator queries its own
   machine id, or a second pool object - the probe does not log its rcx/rdx, which is the
   gap to close.
 - NO EVALUATOR ACTIVATION. track_set fired once per machine and ONLY from 0xC18472, the
   post-release self-set - never from 0xC174AA, the evaluator's activation site. Same
   shape as p2-153, unchanged by c4.
 - cond5 UNMOVED. 300 FAIL-cond5 samples AFTER the write (t>=300607), f38=0x00 bit4=0
   every time; `bit4=1` appears zero times in the whole run. maskB reached 0x3 (genuinely
   paired, 20.235 R3 gate honoured). Exactly as the brief's GRAPHICS DELTA pre-stated: no
   second guardian, and its absence is not a result.

### RESULT 4 - THE INSTRUMENT ITSELF (what made this readable)
All three hooks attached=1. pool_disp emitted one line per DISTINCT type rather than
spending a budget on early noise - the design decision that let the type-45 call at
mac call=57 / rig call=17 be seen at all. The poolc4 probe dumping the WHOLE array on
enter AND leave is what separated "handler never ran" from "ran and wrote nothing" from
"wrote a row we were not watching" - p2-154 could not tell those apart. The type-30
positive control did NOT fire (t30_handler calls=0): the fork sends no type-30 body in
this scenario, so the control is UNEXERCISED, not failed - it neither validates nor
invalidates the hook, and pool_disp's nine other live types carry the "the hook works"
burden instead. Recorded rather than glossed.

### RESULT 5 - VERDICT AND THE NEXT LEVER (behavioural, per the brief's outcome table)
Outcome (c): c4 = 1 achieved and the evaluator still does not activate. The front is now
"WHICH row/pool does the evaluator read", and it has a BEHAVIOURAL answer that needs no
new front: mark EVERY known machine id, not just the peer's. The type-45 body's count
field is 6 bits and the multi-id encoding is already femu-verified (lane E CLAIM 7,
count=2 exact for both mids), so p2-156 sends self+peer in one body on every peer-bearing
push. Whichever row the evaluator queries then reads 1, and the ambiguity of R3 closes by
construction rather than by another instrument. RIDING FREE (observation may be bundled):
give track_c4 the pool+mid probe so the evaluator's own query is logged.

## 20.249 *** p2-156: MARKING THE CLIENT'S OWN MACHINE ID CRASHED THE MAC AND KEPT THE RIG
## *** OUT OF THE TOWER - AND THE c4query PROBE RETIRES THE PREMISE THE WHOLE c4 FRONT WAS
## *** BUILT ON: EACH CLIENT'S +0x602C4 READER ASKS ONLY ABOUT ITS **OWN** MACHINE ID.
## *** 20.245's "the evaluator was blocked by +0x602C4=0" IS THEREFORE SUSPECT: that abort
## *** IS THE SELF ENTRY BEING HANDLED CORRECTLY, NOT THE PEER BEING GATED.
## *** (2026-09-01 18:5x, VERIFIED-BY-EXECUTION + LOGS, logindex p2156crash.db)

### RESULT 1 - THE PROBE'S ANSWER, AND IT IS NOT THE ONE THE FRONT ASSUMED
The p2-156 instrument logged the READER'S QUESTION for the first time. Across both
machines there are exactly TWO distinct (pool, machine id) pairs, one per client:
  mac (mac:1783) t=85360  pool=0x1D2FF980    asks_mid=0x88CB5281391A82CB  = THE MAC's OWN id
  rig (rig:1870) t=99469  pool=0x1E39BE1F980 asks_mid=0x846C8338F7D022E6  = THE RIG's OWN id
Each client asks 0x1404F7680 about ITSELF and nothing else. The pool is the SAME object
that holds the tracking rows (not the second pool of 20.248 R2), so chain mark L5 of the
p2-156 brief is answered and closed: the reader is reachable, we simply had the wrong
model of what it is asking.
CONSEQUENCE, stated plainly: 20.245 R3 read the evaluator's `al=0` return as "the peer is
not contactable, so the evaluator aborts". If the only query is about the client's own
identity, that abort is the SELF entry being skipped - correct, expected, and nothing to
do with the peer. The entire c4 lever (p2-154, p2-155, p2-156) was aimed at a byte whose
zero value we never established was wrong. 20.245 R3 is SUSPECT and 20.246 R6's "c4 is the
evaluator's last hard input" rests on it. Neither is retracted outright here - the
disassembly still says the activation block reads that byte - but the live query set says
the byte it reads is the self entry's, and no boot has ever observed a query for a peer.

### RESULT 2 - THE HARM, AND THE SEQUENCE (mac)
p2-156 sent {peer, self}. On the mac the body arrived while the array held ONE row - the
client's own - so the only thing it did was mark SELF:
  t=230982 (mac:48022) poolc4 enter pool=0x1D2FF980 rows=1 | r0 mid=<mac> c4=0x00
  t=230983 (mac:48023) poolc4 leave                 rows=1 | r0 mid=<mac> c4=0x01   <-- SELF
  t=230985 track_add adds the RIG's row; retail "Could not find tracking data for peer '1'"
  t=230986 track_fixup ret=0x0 -> "Sending peer-reservation release" (the designed
           lifecycle of 20.245, unchanged)
  t=231734 retail: "Received join result from AH ... [session id <BLANK>]" and
           "activity_host_changed: instance=PRIVATE CURRENT, ah-sid=<BLANK>,
           zombie-instance-nonce=0"   <-- THE ACTIVITY CLIENT LOSES ITS HOST
  t=231735 retail: "unknown message type '17'", "unknown message type '52'" - types this
           same client had been dispatching all boot (both are in pool_disp's live set)
  t=231767 retail: private_repair advances create_activity_client -> world_transition
  t=231782 LAST LINE. Process gone (user reports a Wine debugger crash).
RIG: never reached the Tower - repeated "Failed to find the Orbit slice-set name ...
falling back to a new character" (rig:2551, rig:2634), matchmaking aborted, orbit
transition; the user reports a baboon kick. Its counters are abnormal too: track_set
calls=14 and track_fixup calls=13 where p2-155 had 1 (rig:2671/2670).

### RESULT 3 - ATTRIBUTION, HONESTLY BOUNDED
CAUSE (INFERRED, not proven): asserting c4=1 for the client's OWN identity. The byte is a
claim that a machine is a remote peer worth contacting; the client's own logic excludes
self by construction (the construction gate's cond 2 is literally "i != self index",
20.229), so telling it that IT is contactable is a state it is not built to hold.
EVIDENCE FOR: p2-155 ran a long, stable, genuinely paired dwell with the SAME client
instrument family and peer-only marking; p2-156 changed exactly one behavioural thing -
adding self to the body - and both clients failed within one dwell. The mac's symptoms are
PROTOCOL-STATE corruption (host lost, blank session id, previously-handled message types
rejected), not the signature of a wild pointer read.
NOT EXCLUDED: p2-156 also swapped track_c4's probe from retwatch to c4query, which
dereferences rdx. Against it: that probe ran through thousands of calls (census 1,684 by
t=123044) before any trouble, and a bad dereference crashes at the dereference rather than
producing "unknown message type 17". It remains a second variable and is named as one.
THE DISCRIMINATOR, cheap: re-run peer-only with the same client build. Stable = self
marking was the cause; unstable = the probe is, and the probe comes out.

### RESULT 4 - MY ERRORS IN THIS BOOT (both mine, both recorded)
 (a) THE DESIGN. "Mark every id so the row question becomes moot" treated the byte as an
     inert hint. It is an assertion the client acts on, and the one id that must never
     carry it is the client's own. A behavioural change should not have been widened to a
     value class (self) that no evidence said was safe - p2-155 had marked ONLY peers.
 (b) THE LOG LINE. The server printed `ids=2` unconditionally while the appender deduped;
     in the degenerate self-peer case it claimed two ids for a one-id body. I spotted this
     mid-boot and let it stand rather than rebuild - it did not affect the paired reading,
     but a line that overstates what went on the wire is exactly the class of defect this
     project has burned boots on. Fixed with the revert: the line now prints the real count.

### RESULT 5 - STATE AND THE NEXT MOVE
IMMEDIATE: pool_c4_mark_push flipped to FALSE and the server restarted - the bind line
reads `c4_mark_push=0 peer_retry_cap=2`, verified. Source reverted to PEER-ONLY (a
one-element list) so the capability survives without the harmful shape; the ids log line
now reports the true count. Nothing is deployed with self-marking.
THE FRONT IS NOT "make c4 nonzero" ANY MORE. The open question is R1's: does anything ever
read the PEER's contactable byte? Two answers, both cheap:
 (i) the c4query set is already the instrument - it needs a PAIRED dwell to say whether a
     second (pool, mid) pair ever appears. p2-156 crashed before pairing, so the question
     is unanswered rather than answered negatively.
 (ii) if the query set stays self-only through a full paired dwell, the c4 front is DEAD
     and 20.245 R3 / 20.246 R6 are retracted, which puts the peer-render front back on
     cond5 alone (20.246 R7's dynamic write-watch) with the tracking cluster fully
     exonerated rather than half-suspected.

### RESULT 1 - SCENARIO VALIDITY, ESTABLISHED BEFORE ANYTHING WAS READ (20.235 R3)
mac ptable: maskA=0x00020002 maskB=0x00000003 maskC=0x00000003, self=0,
selfRef=0x88CB5281391A82CB. First paired sample t=151280 (mac:15683), 302 samples at
maskB=0x3, still paired at t=260827. A real sustained dwell, not a blip - p2-156's failure
to pair at all is exactly why it answered nothing, and that is not the case here.

### RESULT 2 - THE ANSWER: NOTHING EVER ASKS ABOUT THE PEER
The complete c4query set for the whole boot, both machines, is TWO pairs:
  rig (rig:1784) t=75625  pool=0x1F15874F980 asks_mid=0x846C8338F7D022E6 = THE RIG's OWN
  mac (mac:1911) t=123929 pool=0x1D2FF980    asks_mid=0x88CB5281391A82CB = THE MAC's OWN
The probe emits one line per DISTINCT (pool, machine id) pair with a 16-entry table, so a
third pair at ANY point in the boot would have printed. None did. Meanwhile the reader was
demonstrably live THROUGH and AFTER the paired window - track_c4 census 5,214 (t=242077)
-> 5,662 (t=257088) -> 6,131 (t=272098), i.e. ~900 calls during the paired samples alone.
Roughly six thousand reads, zero of them about the other machine.

### RESULT 3 - AND THE PEER'S BYTE WAS SET THE WHOLE TIME, UNREAD
Peer-only marking worked exactly as p2-155 proved, on both sides:
  rig t=75734 (rig:1833/1834) leave: r0 mid=<rig, own> c4=0x00 | r1 mid=<mac> c4=0x00 -> 0x01
  mac t=255850 (mac:54989/54990) leave: r0 mid=<mac, own> c4=0x00 | r1 mid=<rig> c4=0x00 -> 0x01
Each client's OWN row stayed 0x00 (the p2-156 revert took - `ids=1` on every server push
and `self_machine` absent from the log entirely), and each PEER row went to 1. So for the
whole paired dwell the byte the last three boots existed to set WAS set, on both machines,
and the only function known to read it never looked at it.

### RESULT 4 - THE RETRACTIONS

This is "no peer query IN THIS SCENARIO", not "no peer query exists". Both clients stood in

The peer-render problem is now ONE front, not two. Everything in the tracking/admission

### RESULT 2 - THE LOCAL LOOP IS SELF-ONLY BY DESIGN (the other door, closed)
The creation loop 0x1413086E0's gate 2 ([record+0x818] == local identity) is an OWNERSHIP
test, and the owner field carries each member's OWN identity wherever it has ever been
seen populated:
  mac live (20.221 R1): the PEER's record carried 0x846C8338F7D022E6 = the RIG's own
  identity handle - not the mac's, not garbage;

  (0x846C8338F7D022E6) and rec1=MAC (0xF5D3535B98AEB768) - the same two handles,
  symmetric across machines.
Retail therefore never renders a peer by making its guardian "yours": your record says
you, their record says them, and the loop correctly builds only yours. Reading (b) of
20.221 R4 ("+0x818 becomes the local identity under an authority hand-off") has no
positive evidence and now has design evidence AGAINST it. NOTE: +0x818 flickers on the
local record (7,329 populated / 4,543 zero, 20.221 R1) and reads 0x00 in the p2-146 dump
(a late/post-teardown capture, 20.246 R4) - the field is transient; the populated VALUE
is the datum, and it was always owner==self.

### RESULT 3 - VERDICT
Two doors, both gated on the peer: the local build needs ownership (never true for a
peer, by design), replication needs a receiver (never constructed - cond5). 20.246 R5's
remaining shape (ii) is discharged: the cond5-gated construction IS on the required path
to a rendered peer, and the local-guardian "renders at zero" observation does not
transfer (the local guardian needs no replication - it is locally owned and built by the
ownership-gated loop). THE WRITE-WATCH ON record+0x38 IS THE VALIDATED FRONT.

### RESULT 2 - THE WRITER IS A WHOLESALE TABLE-IMAGE REFRESH (all verified-by-reading)

    - chkstk-allocates 0x59290 bytes ON THE STACK (a full table image),
    - backs the CURRENT table up to the stack (call 1),
    - copies the INCOMING image INTO the live table (call 2: rdx=arg3 image, rcx=table+0x80),
    - sets byte[rbx+0x70]=1.
  0x1403CB340 is called from 0x1404F78E7 inside THE POOL CTOR 0x1404F77D0:
    `mov rdx,[rsp+0x70]` (the ctor's stack ARGUMENT = the image pointer)
    `lea r8,[rsi+0x6C38]` (THE PARTICIPANT TABLE - same anchor as the ptable probe)
    `call 0x1403CB340`.
CONSEQUENCE: no client code computes bit 4 - the gate byte ARRIVES as part of a wholesale
table image consumed at pool construction. 20.246's static closure stands (the copier is a
movups loop, invisible to every store-encoding scan) and 20.238's framing is STRENGTHENED:
the client renders what a server-side image tells it. The masks (maskA/maskB/maskC at
+0x59248/4C/50) ride in the same image - the five-condition gate's inputs are ALL image
fields, refreshed together. The two-tables-swap behavior (20.230 R2) is this backup/restore
pair: the stack copy IS the swap mechanism.

0x1403CB340 re-read with arg mapping pinned: it copies FROM the live table INTO a staging

The ctor's caller (0x140BFE2F0 region, fragment 0x140BFE36D chained) calls 0x1412AADF0 -

layer is the missing half of 20.220's corollary ("the index must ARRIVE FROM OUTSIDE") -
this is the arrival mechanism's infrastructure.

### RESULT 3 - THE STAGING OBJECT AND ITS 21 CONSUMERS
X = 0x140E91EC0(image_id) - a checkout of a per-activity snapshot managed by
0x140C21FE0 (CONTROL-FLOW FLATTENED, encrypted-global registry at ~0x1427F46E8 - the
obfuscator wall; do not statically chase it). 21 checkout sites, three clusters:
  - the pool ctor (publish, above);
  - pool QUERY paths: 0x1404F55B0 reads snapshot [X+0x5C] and does 13-bit entity-index
    arithmetic (0x1FFF mask) - the snapshot is a queryable record-state store;
  - manager clusters 0x1416BC33E (x5) and 0x141741130 (x4): 0x141741130 checks out FOUR
    snapshots from a manager object (fields +0x2A40/+0x2A48/+0x2A68/+0x2B48/+0x2C28/
    +0x2D08 - the "manager array rsi+0x2a00, stride 0x2d0" of 20.215 R2) and passes all
    four to 0x140092D40. These are the consume/apply candidates.
ENCODEDS: E8/E9 both .text + xref_scan --ptrs for every call target named above.

### RESULT 4 - THE FRONT, REFINED
The client's table is CLIENT-LOCAL at birth (gate bytes 0), then published into the
snapshot. In retail, bit 4 must reach the table AFTER birth - either the authority's
snapshot state is transferred to non-authority clients (snapshot = the sharing layer the
pool protocol rides on), or a later apply path writes the table directly. The fork
implements the server side of the pool protocol and has NO participant-table model today
(grep: 0x2AC0/0x6C38 appear in no server source) - if the snapshot delta crosses the
wire, the fork neither forwards nor fabricates it. THE QUESTION THAT MATTERS: which
snapshot consumer WRITES participant-record data back into a table (or into a snapshot
field the gate reads), and is its input wire-sourced? Candidates in order:
  (a) 0x140092D40 (the four-snapshot consumer) + the 0x1416BC33E cluster - read next;
  (b) a targeted rig probe: hook 0x1403CB340 (clean .pdata function, small) to log
      publish direction + content on BOTH machines, plus the watch (with capture-then-
      quiet) on the SNAPSHOT's gate byte - discriminates "snapshot updated from outside"
      in one paired boot.

### RESULT 5 - NO BOOT SPENT; CRASH NOTE STANDS
All of this entry is offline. The p2-158 crash (20.252 R4) remains undetermined; the
watch does not re-boot without the capture-then-quiet mitigation.

at table+0x38 (SELF) and table+0x2AF8 (PEER) - 0x2AC0 apart, both only coverable if

RESTORE invocation - a full-table image copied INTO the live table - through a caller that
is NOT the ctor's publish call. The restore's SOURCE was 0x00 at both gate bytes.

### RESULT 2 - THE RESTORE CALLER IS AN OBFUCATED THUNK (the wall, named)
0x1403CB340 has a second entry: a thunk at 0x1403CB790 (`mov rcx,[rcx+0x10]; jmp
0x1403CB340`) - arg1 becomes [obj+0x10], so dest = [obj+0x10]+0x80... and the surrounding

SECOND .text (obfuscated). The restore's source provenance is behind the obfuscator wall

The consumer clusters from 20.253 R3 were read: 0x140092D40 is a 0x100-byte serializer of
four snapshot HANDLES (a sending shape); 0x1416BC33E is a floats+TLS telemetry-flavored
reader. Neither writes participant records.

### RESULT 3 - THE p2-159 PROBE (designed, not built - ship with capture-then-quiet)
Hook 0x1403CB340 (clean .pdata function start, ~0xDB bytes - verify_hook_rvas gate):
log on enter (a) arg1/arg2/arg3 (dest-object, image-id, src-image), (b) the SOURCE
image's gate bytes for records 0..3 at src+0x38+i*0x2AC0 (the copy is offset-1:1, so the
source's gate bytes map directly), (c) caller RVA. This distinguishes publish (src=table)
from restore (dest=table) per call, names the restore source's gate-byte content, and -
in a PAIRED dwell - shows whether the restore source EVER carries bit4=1 on the
non-authority machine (the retail mechanism) vs never (our fork's gap).
CLI-side, one variable: this plus the existing wwatch (capture-then-quiet) is the whole boot.

### RESULT 4 - FRONT STATE
The restore path is the conduit through which bit4 reaches the table in retail; its source
is obfuscated-static. The fork-side question ("is the restore source wire-fed?") is now
one probe boot from an answer, and the snapshot/publish machinery (20.253) is the
infrastructure it would ride. The client-side "no writer" closure of 20.246 is superseded
in KIND: a writer exists (the restore), it was invisible to every store-encoding scan
because it is a bulk SSE copy dispatched from obfuscated code.

## 20.256 *** THE TYPE-12 DECODE CHAIN, MAPPED TO THE SCHEMA LAYER: BODY -> STREAM ***
## *** -> 13-BIT ENTITY-INDEX REGISTRY WALK -> SCHEMA-DRIVEN APPLY. THE BYTE MAP IS ***
## *** DATA-DRIVEN; THE EXACT EXTRACTOR IS FEMU. (2026-09-02, VERIFIED-BY-READING) ***

### RESULT 1 - THE CHAIN (every hop read)
  type-12 body (4112 B, fork-built)
    -> body header: [body+4] = size dword, [body+8] = payload pointer
       (0x140412A40: stream-wrapped via 0x140351D90 over [body+8]/[body+4])
    -> 0x140412A40(ecx=byte[body], rdx=body, r8d=global-dword, r9=&image_id):
       0x1404C7BC0(ebx, id) then 0x1404C74B0 -> 0x1404C1930
    -> 0x1404C1930: THE 13-BIT ENTITY-INDEX SPACE (dword splits into >>13 and &0x1FFF -
       the same 8192-slot arithmetic as the entity-slot machinery) walks a registry
       (global -> table -> entry+0x48 -> object) keyed by the index, then applies:
       0x1404BD2A0 (with [rcx+0x18] count-gated variant) / 0x1404BEE90
    -> 0x1404BD2A0 -> 0x1404B7E10 -> deeper: SCHEMA-DRIVEN field application into the
       table-layout image (the same decode family as svc22's 0x1404DC080).
  The image the 0x1416E6250 path publishes carries the table layout 1:1 (identity at
  +8, gate byte at +0x38, stride 0x2AC0 - measured live, 20.255 R2).
ENCODEDS: disasm_fn (pdata-bounded) at every hop; no store-encoding claims made.

### RESULT 2 - WHY THE MAPPING IS EMPIRICAL, NOT STATIC
The field mapping lives in the runtime schema registry (data), not in instructions -
the same shape the corpus already cracked ONCE: femu_v2 ran the svc22 apply decoder
(0x1404DC080) against dump state with zero scaffolding (7/7 acceptance). THE EXTRACTOR:
femu 0x140412A40 (or 0x1404C1930) against a captured type-12 body + dump state, then
DIFF the produced image against the body - the byte map falls out empirically, including
the negative (if no body byte lands at image+0x38, the gate byte is NOT type-12-sourced
and the lever moves to whatever else writes the image).

### RESULT 3 - THE BEHAVIORAL BOOT DESIGN (current best shape)
  1. femu the type-12 decode (offline, no boot) -> the body-to-image byte map.
  2. Fork change: set bit4 in the body field(s) that map to image+0x38 for the peer's
     record - a settings-gated behaviour switch per HARD RULES.
  3. Boot: pubrest (retained, DR-free) verifies f38src bit4=1 on the receiver at the
     message-driven publish; pgate then reports cond5 pass/fail; the receiver
     construction (20.223's vtable group) either appears or the front moves again.
Steps 2-3 are THE behavioral test the session contract calls for.

### RESULT 4 - HONEST LIMITS
(a) The type-12 attribution rests on the 20-tick correlation (arrive -> publish) and the
    identities in the image; the router's case-12 handler -> 0x1416E6250 link is not yet
    walked (the handler objects are vtable-dispatched; the vtable group is at
    .rdata 0x141C9F6F0-0x141C9F728). If femu's map shows the gate byte unsourced, first
    re-check the attribution before hunting another message.
(b) The schema registry's runtime state must come from a dump that entered the same

### RESULT 3 - THE 0x140412A40 ABI, CORRECTED (disasm of the 160 B wrapper)
  0x140412A40(ecx=KEY, rdx=body_obj, r8d=INDEX, r9=&image_id):
    ebx = r8d
    0x140351D90(&stream, [body+8], [body+4])   ; stream over payload+size (20.256 R1 right)
    0x14034C290(&stream)                       ; stream init
    0x1404C7BC0(ecx=KEY, rdx=&image_id)        ; KEY RESOLVER (no .pdata - obfuscated)
    0x1404C74B0(ecx=INDEX, &stream, &id, &id, 0) -> 0x1404C1930
    0x14034EB90(&stream)                       ; stream destroy
  20.256 R1's "ecx=byte[body]" is SUPERSEDED: ecx is the type-12 schema key
  (the 0x808086A8 family), r8d is the packed 13-bit entity index. The wrapper
  hardcodes its own [rsp+0x20]=0, which flows through 0x1404C74B0's [rsp+0x60]
  into 0x1404C1930's count gate ([rsp+0x5b0]) -> the wrapper's path selects the
  0x1404BEE90 apply variant, not 0x1404BD2A0.

### RESULT 4 - THE REGISTRY WALK, READ (0x1404C1930 = walk+apply, 380 B; its
### sibling 0x1404C4BA0, 262 B, is the same walk inside the resolver path)
  table = [[.data 0x142439C70]]                ; heap ptr, dump value 0x22202C669B8
  entry = table + (((idx>>13 | 0xffc0000)>>0x12) & ((idx>>13)&0xFFFF)) << 6
  row   = [entry+8] + [entry+0x30] * (idx & 0x1FFF)
  elem  = row - ([entry+0x34] & [row+8]) + 0x48
  obj   = [elem] ? [elem] + elem : 0           ; offset-encoded pointer
  then apply: count gate ? 0x1404BD2A0(obj,&ctx) : 0x1404BEE90(obj,&ctx)
  For index<2^31 with (idx>>13)<2^18 the entry select reduces to (idx>>13)&0x3FF.
  Key 0x808086A8 selects entry 0x404 (page present in dump per minidump_reader).

  stride(+0x30)=0 mask(+0x34)=0 and its object link [row_base+0x48] = NULL.
  Consistent with PROVENANCE (rig solo/teardown at dump time). Consequence: the
  walk cannot hit a live object from dump state alone - the map run must GRAFT
  a target record and re-wire an entry (wmem), or find the live image elsewhere.

### RESULT 6 *** THE POSITIVE REFERENCE - AND IT UNDERCUTS THE cond5 PREMISE ***
The peer image contains a RENDERED participant (record 0, the local player) and a
NON-RENDERED one (record 1, the rig) side by side. Diffing the two records against each
other - not against another image - is the first POSITIVE reference this front has had:

  record size 0x2AC0 = 10,944 bytes.  THEY DIFFER IN 31 BYTES, 10 RUNS.
  +0x0000  self=05                peer=00     <- the ONLY byte set in self and zero in peer
  +0x0008  self=cb821a398152cb88  peer=e622d0f738836c84   (identities - both populated)
  +0x0018  self=4fff62141a041d00  peer=1dbb80a2adf6f268   (both populated)

  +0x00CA  self=10 peer=11 | +0x00D8 self=01 peer=03 | +0x00DA self=10 peer=11

TWO CONSEQUENCES, and the second is the important one:
 (a) The two records are STRUCTURALLY THE SAME. Every field populated in self is populated

     self's +0x00 moving 0x03 -> 0x05 when the peer arrived, so +0x00 is a per-record state

     boot since it was written (p2-150: 603 mac i=0 samples, all f38=0x00) and that line
     was read as a peer problem every time.
 STATUS: (b) is VERIFIED-BY-EXECUTION as a measurement (self's +0x38 is 0x00 while self is
 on screen). Its INTERPRETATION - that cond5 gates something other than the render - is
 INFERRED and is the next thing to test; 20.251's "the cond5-gated receiver is REQUIRED to
 render a peer" is the claim now in tension and must be re-read before anything is built on

## 20.259 *** cond5 IS NOT THE RENDER GATE. THE BIT WAS FORCED SET ON THE PEER RECORD, ***
## *** ALL TRACKED CONDITIONS PASSED FOR 294 CONSECUTIVE WALKS, AND NOTHING RENDERED ***
## *** AND NOTHING WAS CONSTRUCTED. THE +0x38 FRONT IS DEAD. ***
## *** (2026-09-02, p2-161, VERIFIED-BY-EXECUTION) ***

### RESULT 1 - THE EXPERIMENT AND ITS OUTCOME
Client-side THROWAWAY DIAGNOSTIC (governing constraint: the client is never modified; this
was admissible only to answer "does this byte matter", and gate_poke was reverted to 0 the
moment the result was in). Mac poked, RIG UNPOKED AS CONTROL.
  gatepoke i=1 rec8=0x846C8338F7D022E6 (the rig) f38_was=0x00 -> f38_now=0x10 gate_ok=1
  pgate    i=1 self=0 bit4=1 maskA_bit=1 -> ALL-PASS-would-construct  x294
  server   6 x type-12 body=4095 (peer row), then withdrawn - the standard pattern
  SCREEN:  NOTHING. The user remained alone in the Tower.
  LOG:     not ONE event class appears after the poke that was not already present -
           no receiver construction, no new probe family, nothing.
The byte HELD at 0x10 across all 294 walks, so this is not a race lost to the bulk restore.

### RESULT 2 - WHAT THIS KILLS
The +0x38 / cond5 front. Roughly TEN BOOTS went into hunting a writer for that byte on the
strength of 20.251 ("the cond5-gated receiver is REQUIRED to render a peer"). Setting it
changes nothing. Combined with 20.258 R6 - the RENDERED self record has +0x38 = 0x00, bit 4
CLEAR - the conclusion is that cond5 is not what gates rendering a peer, and 20.251's
claim does not survive as stated. DO NOT RESUME the +0x38 writer hunt.
This also retires the remaining reason to care about the staging image's gate byte, and
with it the last motivation for the femu lane (already closed by 20.258).

### RESULT 3 - HONEST LIMITS (what this does NOT prove)
 (a) pgate's "ALL-PASS" is OUR REIMPLEMENTATION of the conditions, not the game's own
     decision. It proves our model of the gate is satisfied; it does not prove the game
     evaluated that model, at that moment, over that memory.
 (b) THE CONDITION SET IS INCOMPLETE. pgate evaluates cond1 (the maskB present-bit it
     iterates), cond3, cond4 and cond5. THERE IS NO cond2 ANYWHERE IN THE PROBE. Whatever
     condition 2 is, it has never been measured, and "all conditions pass" has always meant
     "all conditions we implemented pass".
 (c) The decider may read the STAGING IMAGE rather than the live table. We poked the table
     only; the image's +0x38 stayed 0x00 throughout (20.258). A construction check that
     reads the image would not have seen the poke.
 (b) and (c) are the two ways cond5 could still matter. Both are cheap to settle offline
     and must be settled BEFORE anyone reopens the byte on the strength of a hunch.

### RESULT 4 - WHERE THE FRONT GOES, UNDER THE GOVERNING CONSTRAINT
THE CLIENT IS NEVER MODIFIED; THE SERVER MUST ACCOMPLISH EVERYTHING (AGENTS.md). The
method that has actually produced results twice running is the POSITIVE REFERENCE: compare
the thing that works against the thing that does not, in our own environment.
  - The local player RENDERS. It is the only working example of a rendered participant we
    have, and 20.258 R6 showed its record is structurally identical to the peer's.
  - So the difference that matters is NOT in the participant record. Find the path that
    actually renders the local player, and ask what server input would drive that same path
    for a second participant. That is an offline question and it costs no boot.
  - Still open and untouched: 20.256 R4a (the router's case-12 -> 0x1416E6250 link was
    never walked) and +0x00 (20.258 R6's one structural gap) - but +0x00 is now a LOWER
    priority than it looked, because this boot shows record-level condition bytes are not
    what stands between us and a rendered peer.
EVIDENCE: RE_output/logindex/p2161b.db. Brief: RE_output/claims/BOOT_BRIEF_p2-161.md.

## 20.260 *** THE MEMBER LOOP REJECTS THE PEER AT GATE 2, AND GATE 2 IS SELF-BY- ***
## *** CONSTRUCTION: it compares member[+0x818] against a value gate1 fills with THIS ***
## *** MACHINE'S OWN identity - verified on BOTH machines across THREE boots. The loop ***
## *** is not the peer path and never could be. NO BOOT SPENT. (2026-09-02) ***

### RESULT 1 - THE LOOP BODY, DISASSEMBLED (0x1413086E0, the creation loop)
  0x141308aa0  mov  ecx,[rsp+0x60]          ; member index
  0x141308aa4  call 0x140B39DC0             ; member_get -> rax -> rdi (the member record)
  0x141308aa9  lea  rcx,[rsp+0x68]          ; rcx = a STACK SLOT, not the member
  0x141308ab1  call 0x1412FBA60             ; gate1(&slot) - fills the slot, returns al
  0x141308ab6  test al,al / je skip         ; GATE 1
  0x141308aba  mov  rax,[rdi+0x818]
  0x141308ac1  cmp  rax,[rsp+0x68]          ; *** GATE 2 ***
  0x141308ac6  sete al / test al,al / je skip
  ...                                        ; only then: 0x1417040F0 (memidx_alloc),
  0x141308b2a  call 0x1416EE180             ; THE CREATOR
  0x141308b44  jne  0x141308aa0             ; next member

### RESULT 2 - WHAT GATE 2 COMPARES, MEASURED ON BOTH SIDES
gate1's out-parameter (the value it writes into [rsp+0x68]) equals THE OBSERVING MACHINE'S
OWN identity, every time, on both machines, in three separate boots:
    p2-150  mac gate1=0xF5D3535B98AEB768  mac selfRef=0xF5D3535B98AEB768
            rig gate1=0x846C8338F7D022E6  rig selfRef=0x846C8338F7D022E6
    p2-153  same pattern     p2-155  mac gate1=0x88CB5281391A82CB = mac selfRef
It is never the other machine's id and never a shared host id. So GATE 2 reads:
    "create an entity for this member ONLY IF member[+0x818] == MY OWN identity."
The loop is therefore SELF-ONLY BY CONSTRUCTION. A peer cannot pass it unless the peer's
member record carries the RECEIVER's identity at +0x818 - a different value in the same
wire field for each recipient, which is not what that field can mean.
This gives 20.251's phrase ("local loop self-only by design") its MECHANISM, and it makes
the design claim testable rather than asserted.

### RESULT 3 - THE PEER IS ITERATED, AND IS REJECTED, NOT SKIPPED
The peer is NOT invisible to the loop: member_get returns the rig's record 2,788 times on
the mac in p2-161. The loop sees it every pass and rejects it at gate 2. Downstream,
idx_alloc records ZERO enter/leave calls for the entire paired window (p2-161: 48 calls at
mgr_free=0 during solo load, 7 successful allocations at t=167297-190962, then NOTHING
after the peer arrives at t=192531). 20.219 R4's measurement is re-verified independently.

### RESULT 4 - THE LOAD-TIME BURST IS SELF, AND ITS CHAIN IS NOW FULLY READ
The ~19-63 `failed to create 'player_broadcast'` failures every boot are the LOCAL player's
own creation, driven by a type-12 push and failing only because the manager is not yet
filled. Captured end to end (p2-161 mac, t=163988-164014):
    pooldisp type=12 -> c4query(self) -> pubrest -> member_get(owner=self) -> gate1 al=1
    -> memidx_alloc out0=0x1FFBA000 -> idx_alloc mgr_free=0 -> out0=0xFFFFFFFF -> "failed"
Once the pool->manager transfer lands, the same chain SUCCEEDS: 7 allocations, mgr_free
150->144. So the chain works; it is simply never entered for a peer.
This settles the 20.208 R6 / 20.213 R1 vs 20.219 R5 dispute: 20.219 R5's "self-allocation
during load" reading is CORRECT (the burst is self, gated on the free pool exactly as
20.213 R1 found), and 20.208 R6's "our injection makes the client try" is TRUE BUT NOT
PEER-RELATED - it provoked the LOCAL player's creation path, not a peer's.

### RESULT 5 - WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT ANSWER
ANSWERED, with mechanism, no boot: why no peer entity is created by THIS loop, and why no
amount of server input to it could change that. The loop is eliminated properly - by its
construction, not by a null observation.
NOT ANSWERED: what DOES create a peer entity. It must be the replication path (the 20.221
cluster / 20.223 receiver group), which is a different entry. 20.251 said that receiver is
cond5-gated and required; 20.259 showed cond5 forced-set changes nothing. Both cannot be

Gate 2 (`cmp [rdi+0x818], [rsp+0x68]`, 20.260) asks "IS THIS MEMBER MINE?". For a peer the

0x1413086E0 is the LOCAL-AUTHORITY entity creator and is behaving exactly as designed.
THIS IS NOT A LEVER, AND IT MUST NOT BE MADE ONE. Forcing it would require the server to
tell each client that the PEER belongs to THEM - a different value in the same wire field
per recipient - which would make the client build a LOCALLY-OWNED, LOCALLY-SIMULATED
duplicate of a remote player rather than a replicated peer. That is not the retail
mechanism and it would be wrong even if it drew something on screen. Under the governing
constraint (the client is never modified; the server must accomplish everything) it is also
not something the server can coherently express.

### RESULT 1 - THE DISCRIMINATOR: THE SUCCESSFUL SET IS BOOT-INVARIANT
Successful registrations (memidx_alloc -> idx_publish) across six boots:
    p2-150 mac 8/8   rig 7/8       p2-153 mac 8/8   rig 7/7
    p2-155 mac 8/8   rig 7/7       p2-157 mac 8/8   rig 7/7
    p2-160 mac 8/8                 p2-161 mac 8/8
EIGHT on the mac, SEVEN on the rig, EVERY BOOT - independent of run length, of whether a

counters (pb_create / idx_alloc / ent_make) swing 7 / 25 / 33 / 49 / 50 / 51 / 52 / 55:
those are the load-burst FAILURES, whose count depends only on how long the burst ran
before the pool->manager transfer landed.
A fixed per-machine count that never moves is the signature of THE CLIENT'S OWN ENTITY SET
(guardian, ghost, ship/sparrow, camera rig and the like). World or ambient actors would
vary with place and time; Tower NPCs would vary between runs; a peer would add one. None
of that happens. The mac's extra one over the rig is stable too and is most likely the
in-process server host object, though that is INFERRED, not measured.

### RESULT 2 - THE REGISTRATION PATH, READ END TO END
    0x1403F8580 / 0x140404310  ->  0x1404D7110  ->  0x1404D7330 (the registrar)
    0x1404D7330:  test byte [rcx+0x124],1        ; registerable?
                  cmp  dword [rcx+0x110],-1      ; index not yet assigned?
                  call 0x1403BD530 / 0x1403BD5B0 ; obtain an index -> eax
                  mov  [rbx+0x110],eax           ; STORE THE INDEX ON THE OBJECT
                  call 0x1403BD6B0(eax, [obj+0xC0])   ; publish
    0x1403BD6B0 loads a global and tail-dispatches - which is why the idx_publish probe
    logs caller_rva=0x4D7375 (the return address in 0x1404D7330) rather than a direct call
    site. 0x1404D7110 masks the object's 13-bit index (`and ecx,0x1FFF`, [obj+0x120]).
    Callers: 0x1403F8580 <- 0x1403FDB82 / 0x140403290 ; 0x140404310 <- 0x140C1548B.
Object shape: +0xC0 payload, +0x110 assigned index, +0x120 13-bit index, +0x124 flags
(bit 0 = registerable, 0x280 mask tested at entry), +0x12C a stored byte.

### RESULT 3 *** THE CONCLUSION, AND IT IS A HARD ONE ***
Every entity this build has ever successfully created is LOCALLY OWNED and belongs to a
fixed per-machine set. Combined with 20.263 (the codec cluster ent_recv/ent_header/
ent_create has never executed for anything) and 20.223 (no receiver instance in 6.49 GB):
    THIS BUILD HAS NEVER, IN ANY BOOT WE HAVE LOGS FOR, RENDERED AN ENTITY IT DOES NOT OWN.
Therefore THE POSITIVE REFERENCE DOES NOT EXIST IN OUR ENVIRONMENT. The method that broke
open 20.260/20.261 - compare the working case against the broken one - CANNOT be applied to
replication, because we have never once observed replication working, for a peer or for
anything else.
This is the fact 20.263 R5 named as the second branch, and it is the branch we are on.

## 20.265 *** ALL FOUR "INSTALLER" CALLERS ARE TEARDOWN. THE RECEIVER TABLE HAS EXACTLY ***
## *** ONE INSERT SITE IN THE WHOLE BINARY, AND IT IS GATED BY A SINGLE OBFUSCATED ***
## *** PREDICATE 0x1416CA0B0. THAT PREDICATE IS THE FRONT. (2026-09-02, NO BOOT) ***

### RESULT 1 *** A DIRECTION ERROR IN 20.223: 0x1416CACD0 IS CALLED ONLY ON TEARDOWN ***
20.223 R1 named 0x1416CACD0 "the receiver-vtable installer" (it stores four interior
addresses of the vtable group into one object), and 20.251 R1 used its four callers as the
scan ORACLE. All four callers were disassembled this session and every one is the SAME
sequence - a removal:
    if ([entry+0x48] != 0) { rdi=[entry+0x50]; 0x1416E9E50(entry);
                             [container + rdi*8 + 0x178] = 0; dec [container+0x170]; }
    0x1416E9CF0(entry);  0x1416CACD0(entry)
      callers: 0x1416FFDEE (in 0x1416FFD60), 0x1416FFE55 (0x1416FFE4A),
               0x1417026D3 (0x141702595), 0x141709D96 (0x141709D30)
Detach, clear the slot, decrement the count, then two calls. In C++ that trailing pair is a
destructor chain, and writing vptrs is what a destructor does as the hierarchy unwinds.
CONSEQUENCE: the four calls are the WRONG END OF THE LIFECYCLE. The receiver's actual
CONSTRUCTOR has never been located, and every prior statement of the form "the installer's
callers are X" describes destruction. This does NOT invalidate 20.223 R3's measurement (no
object in 6.49 GB carries those secondary vptrs - still true, still the key fact) nor
20.251 R1's scan mechanics (the oracle worked; only its label was wrong).

### RESULT 2 - THE CONTAINER, AND ITS ONE DOOR
The four teardown sites and the insert site share one structure:
    container +0x170 = live count      +0x178 = 32 entry pointers (slots 0..0x1F)
    entry     +0x44 = a flag byte      +0x48 = a pointer   +0x50 = its own slot index
Byte-pattern scan over BOTH .text for `inc/dec dword [reg+0x170]`:
    INSERT: exactly ONE site, 0x1416FF44E (inside 0x1416FF3C0)
    REMOVE: five sites - 0x140BC981B, 0x1416FFDDD, 0x1416FFE3F, 0x1417026C2, 0x141709D85
ONE way in, five ways out, in the entire image.

### RESULT 3 *** THE GATE: 0x1416FF3C0's INSERT IS DECIDED BY ONE CALL ***
    0x1416FF3C0(rcx=container, rdx, r8d, r9):
      lea  rcx,[rsp+0x40]
      call 0x1416CA0B0            ; *** THE PREDICATE ***
      cmp  eax,-1
      je   0x1416FF45C            ; -1 -> RETURN, NO ENTRY, NO RECEIVER, NOTHING
      ...  0x1416EBD30(...)       ; build the entry
      scan slots 0..0x1F of [rbx+i*8+0x178] for a free one, store it
      inc  [rbx+0x170]            ; 0x1416FF44E
      0x1416E8200(rdx=rbx)
If 0x1416CA0B0 returns -1, the table never gains an entry - and 20.223 R3 measured that in
6.49 GB it never has. This is the first single, named decision point the project has found
on receiver creation.

### RESULT 4 - THE PREDICATE IS OBFUSCATED AND MUST BE MEASURED, NOT READ
0x1416CA0B0 is pdata-bounded 0x1416CA0B0..0x1416CAAF9 (~2.6 KB) and is in the known
obfuscation family:
  - reads an encrypted global at rip+0x1987ED5 = **0x143051FA8**; null -> branches away;
  - calls into the virtualised second .text (0x1472B4425, 0x146260781, 0x144F9D1FB);
  - carries the constants 0x52343BC7 / 0x97603F4F / 0xF08BF267 - and 0x97603F4F /
    0xF08BF267 are EXACTLY the r8/r9 values the live memidx_alloc probe logs every boot,
    so this is the same subsystem as the working entity-registration path (20.264 R2).
Static reading will not answer it, for the same reason 20.220's two components and 20.246
R7's runtime-registered writer could not be read. IT MUST BE MEASURED.

## 20.266 *** THE GLOBAL IS NOT NULL - THE PRECONDITION HOLDS. femu CANNOT RESOLVE ***
## *** 0x1416CA0B0: IT IS CONTROL-FLOW-FLATTENED WITH PER-RUN KEYED POINTER DECRYPTION, ***
## *** AND BOTH DUMPS FAIL IDENTICALLY. THE ONE-PROBE BOOT IS NOW EARNED. (2026-09-02) ***

### RESULT 1 - THE GLOBAL AT 0x143051FA8 IS POPULATED IN BOTH PAIRED DUMPS
    p2-146  86 15 EE 2A 54 2E EC 2B | 78 B0 99 58 F7 7F 00 00
    p2-150  ED AC E1 FE 04 33 AD B6 | 78 B0 99 58 F7 7F 00 00
The first qword DIFFERS between dumps; the qword after it is IDENTICAL
(0x00007FF75899B078, module RVA 0x29B078). That is the signature of an OBFUSCATED POINTER:
the stored value is the real pointer XORed with per-run keys, sitting next to a stable
neighbour. So 0x1416CA0B0's first branch (`test rdi,rdi; je`) is NOT the reason it fails -
the subsystem object exists in both paired-Tower captures. The bail is deeper.

### RESULT 2 - WHAT THE FUNCTION ACTUALLY IS (refines 20.265 R3)
Read at its call site rather than assumed: after `call 0x1416CA0B0`, 0x1416FF3C0 does
`mov rcx,[rsp+0x40]` and uses it as an OBJECT, while eax is compared to -1 and later passed
as `edx` to the entry builder. So:
    0x1416CA0B0(rcx = &out_object) -> eax = an INDEX, *out = an OBJECT, -1 = FAILURE
It is an ALLOCATOR ("give me a receiver slot/object"), NOT a permission predicate. -1 means
the allocation did not happen, which is a different question from "we were not allowed".
This matters for the probe design and for what a negative would mean.

### RESULT 3 - WHY femu CANNOT ANSWER IT (the pre-named condition of 20.265 R5, met)
    femu --selftest: PASS (oracle green, L1-L4).
    0x1416CA0B0 on p2-150: crash:read-beyond-image at rip=0x1416CA421, rdi=0x89A43741DFB98
    0x1416CA0B0 on p2-146: crash:read-beyond-image at rip=0x1416CA421, rdi=0x987133D5C5FC3
    identical trace both times: ...0x1416CA1CE 1D3 1D6 1DA 413 415 41B 421
Same instruction, both dumps, DIFFERENT garbage - and neither value is a legal user-mode
pointer (>47 bits). The function is control-flow-flattened: a dispatcher at 0x1416CA140,
state carried in ecx and compared against magics (0x177B593D / 0x177BDA9A / 0xAB1F3B47),
with rdi transformed step by step (`rol rdi,0x20` / `xor rdi,rdx` / `ror rdi,0x20`) and
keys drawn from the virtualised second .text (0x1472B4425, 0x146260781, 0x144F9D1FB).
Those keys are per-run and are not reproducible from a dump, so the decryption completes
wrongly and the flattened loop exits early into 0x1416CA421 with an undecrypted rdi.
femu is not broken here - it is being asked for something a dump cannot supply. Its
selftest passing while this fails is exactly the separation an oracle exists to make.

### RESULT 4 - THE PROBE THIS EARNS (design, NOT yet built)
20.265 R5 said a boot is justified ONLY if femu cannot resolve it. It cannot. The probe:
  HOOK 0x1416CA0B0 (pdata-exact 0x1416CA0B0..0x1416CAAF9, a clean function start).
  LOG on enter: rcx (the out-slot address) and the caller RVA.
  LOG on leave: eax (the index, or -1) and *rcx (the object written, or 0).
  ONE contract: does the receiver allocator ever run, and what does it return?
  PRE-NAMED OUTCOMES:
   (a) NEVER CALLED -> the insert path 0x1416FF3C0 is itself never reached, and the front
       moves UP to whoever calls it. The receiver question would then be premature.
   (b) CALLED, returns -1 -> the allocator refuses. That is the first hard measurement of
       the refusal, and its arguments/caller name what to look at next.
   (c) CALLED, returns an index -> an entry IS created, and 20.223's "no instance in
       6.49 GB" needs re-examining (wrong object searched, or torn down before the dump).
  ABSENCE NEGATIVE: zero lines while the client reaches the Tower indicts the hook (the
  function is obfuscated but its ENTRY is a normal prologue; verify_hook_rvas must pass).
  This is observation-only, read-only, no writes into game memory - compliant with the
  governing constraint. It is ONE hook, not a wide net.
EVIDENCE: minidump_reader on both paired dumps at rva 0x3051FA8; femu v2 under miniconda
(selftest PASS) against both dumps; disasm_fn 0x1416CA0B0 / 0x1416FF3C0 (pdata-exact).

## 20.267 *** 20.223's MEASUREMENT SURVIVES MY OWN CHALLENGE TO IT. THE INSERT CHAIN IS ***
## *** ONE CALLER DEEP AT EVERY HOP. THE DUMP DOES NOT HOLD THE ANSWER. (2026-09-02) ***

### RESULT 1 - THE CHALLENGE, AND WHY IT FAILED
20.265 R1 found that 0x1416CACD0 is called only from teardown, which raised a real doubt:
if it is the DESTRUCTOR's vptr write, then 20.223 searched the dump for base/destroyed-state
vptrs and "no receiver instance in 6.49 GB" could be an artifact of the wrong signature.
CHECKED, p2-146: 20.223's single hit, heap object 0x233461F1D90, reads
    +0x00 = 0x7FF75899AD90  (= image 0x141C9AD90, the PRIMARY vptr - 20.223 R1 confirmed)
    +0x08 = 0x23345E04268   +0x18 = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF   +0x40 = 0x7FF75899AD30
    +0xA8, +0x100, +0x140, +0x170..+0x178 region: ALL ZERO
An object carrying the primary vptr and NOTHING at any of the four interface offsets is not
a constructed receiver under either reading - ctor or dtor, a live multiple-inheritance
object has its secondary vptrs. 20.223's conclusion STANDS. My challenge is withdrawn; the
only thing that changes is the LABEL on 0x1416CACD0 (20.265 R1), not the measurement.

### RESULT 2 - THE INSERT CHAIN, TRACED TO ITS TOP (all pdata-exact, all single-caller)
    0x1417039CD  ->  0x1416FF3C0  ->  0x1416CA0B0 (the allocator)   [1 caller each hop]
At the call: rcx = [r15+8] (the container), rdx = rbx+0x2C where rbx = r15 + r12*8,
r8d = r12d (a slot index), r9 = r14. So the container is reached through a parent object
r15 whose +8 holds it, and 0x1417039CD itself opens by iterating the SAME 32-slot table
(`mov rdx,[r8+rax*8+0x178]`, bounds 0..0x1F). One insert site, one caller, one allocator -
the narrowest chain this project has mapped.

### RESULT 3 - THE HONEST LIMIT, STATED PLAINLY
The dump cannot answer whether 0x1416CA0B0 runs or what it returns:
  - it is control-flow-flattened with per-run keyed pointer decryption, and femu fails
    identically on BOTH dumps with different garbage (20.266 R3);
  - the container is reached through a register chain (r15), not a static global, so there
    is no address to read without knowing r15;
  - the table is empty in the dump either way, which is consistent with BOTH "never
    inserted" and "inserted and torn down before capture" - the five remove sites make the
    second reading live, not pedantic.
So this is a genuine measurement limit, not a gap in effort. Recording it as such rather
than proposing an instrument by reflex: what a session does when it hits a limit is the
thing the 09-02 postmortems are about.
EVIDENCE: minidump_reader p2-146 at 0x233461F1D90; E8 caller scans; disasm_fn 0x1417039CD.

the registry is dump-scoped but key-stable - the p2-146 dump is the healthy reference.)

### RESULT 2 - (iv) THE MASK MACHINERY, COMPLETE (every edge verified by disassembly)
THE RECORD'S SHAPE (correction to 20.276's model): the 0x41F0 record embeds THREE
connection objects - rec+0x0000 (state rec+0x1D18), rec+0x00A8 (state rec+0x1DC0, the
guard's predicate-3 object via 0x1417C4230), rec+0x13D0 (state rec+0x30E8, predicate 2's
field!). The record ctor 0x1417BF040 (calls the connection ctor 0x1417BEB20, then zeroes
the extras incl. the dword at obj-B+0x306A = rec+0x3110..0x3115 - all three mask words).
THE GUARD'S TEST (0x1417C40F0, verified firsthand): skip if dword[rec+0x30E8]==0 (the
20.269 "active" check - it is obj C's state!); mask test = `mov dx,1<<bit; test word
[rec+0x3112], dx`; identity test = 0x1403DF020(rec+0x3144, arg4) - 86 bytes, CONDITIONAL
(0x1403EA820 type/parse gate, byte +0x55 in {6,7}, else the virtual comparator).
THE DISOWN SWEEP (0x1417021C0 family, 4 walker passes, runs in the admission path -
this is the already-probed 'ptable' function): pass 1 walks records by bit (0x1417E56C0),
fetches each record's identity (0x1417C4350: SSE-copies rec+0x3144 86 B), walks ALL
participant slots comparing slot+0x142 (0x14187E83E, r8d=0x56) - if NO slot claims the
record: 0x1416FA560 (parallel array update, stride 0x700 @ container+0x5498) +
0x1417C4810 (clears the bit in BOTH rec+0x3112 AND rec+0x3114). Pass 2 checks each slot
is claimed by some record (else the slot-punishment path). Passes 3/4 = THE CLAIM:
0x1417C3480 -> 0x1417C08F0 (find record by 86-byte identity vs the slot's blob, reading
slot+0xEC or slot+0x142 by the slot's +8 kind; no match -> BEST-FREE record for
re-birth) -> flags (or/and byte rec+0x3110) + 24-B copy to rec+0x4280 -> 0x1417C43C0
(bts bit into word rec+0x3114 via obj-B+0x306C - the mask SET) -> 0x1416FA330 +
0x1417C43C0 tail (parallel array).
THE t=328727 EVENT EXPLAINED: the sweep ran on the membership apply, found NO slot
claiming rec2's identity (the blob is blank - W1), and disowned rec2 (bit cleared).
rec1's IMMUNITY EXPLAINED: the slots' blank +0x142 blobs EQUAL rec1's zero identity -
the blank card claims the blank record, so rec1 is never disowned and keeps its bit.
THE BIRTH WORD vs THE CLAIM WORD: the guard tests +0x3112; the claim's bts writes
+0x3114; the birth path sets +0x3112 from the container-at-creation (empirical: rec2
born 0x0020 = container -1 + 6 = bit 5; rec1 born 0x0080 = container 1 + 6 = bit 7).
The cursor/computed nature of the birth write is why no direct +0x3112 set exists in
field_xref (the same blind spot as the composer).

### RESULT 3 - THE CASCADE VERDICT (upgrades 20.279's unknown)
Filling slot+0x142 with the peer's transport identity (the W1 fix) mechanically:
  (1) STOPS the disown of rec2 (its identity becomes claimed) - the record keeps its
      state and bits;
  (2) causes rec1 to be DISOWNED at the next sweep (no slot's non-blank blob matches a
      zero identity anymore) - the guard stops matching the placeholder;
  (3) arms the claim path: the slot's identity now find-or-creates/claims its record
      and sets the required bit (via the birth path on a re-born record, or +0x3114 on
      the existing one).
RESIDUAL PINS (for the boot's outcome tree, not blockers): whether the guard-tested
+0x3112 word gets bit 7 on the CLAIMED EXISTING record vs only on a RE-BORN one
(the birth-path write is cursor-class; prerequisite (i)'s runtime pin + the boot's
first-seen-key leave lines answer it), and the exact 86 bytes to emit (prerequisite
(ii): capture rec+0x3144's full 86 bytes - the probe change already specified).
The observed send ORDER (membership t=328223 -> record birth t=328234 with container=-1)
also flags a SEQUENCING lever: if the peer's slot assignment is visible in the container
before the transport association is born, the record is born with the right bit. The
fork controls that order.
NEXT: prerequisites (i)+(ii) ride the probe rebuild; the encoder change targets
0x808086B2 fields [10]-[12] for the peer member row; then solo control -> paired boot.

### R1 THE SERVER WAS COMPOSING THE WRONG ENDPOINT (source-verified, then fixed)
`activity_membership_push` read the peer card from
`descriptor::read(peerCitizen.descriptor)`. That descriptor is built by
`build_advertisement` and is the ACTIVITY-HOST endpoint FOR A REGION - not the peer's own
transport endpoint. Both directions therefore carried the same address. p2-165's server
log: `addr=3232235940` (192.168.1.164, the mac) on all six builds, INCLUDING the body
whose peer row named the rig (key 0x846C8338F7D022E6). The mac was being told its peer
lived at the mac's own address. A card naming the wrong machine cannot match the
reservation record whatever the compose hop does, so p2-165 could never have observed the
compose question cleanly - only one of the two causes was ever visible.

FIX: `group_host::net_addr_for_member()` returns the peer's OWN NetAddr blob, echoed byte
exact from its connect request via the existing `peer::remote_address()` - the rule
`publish_snapshot` already follows. Absent/ambiguous publishes NOTHING and names the
cause; a wrong endpoint is worse than a blank one, because the sweep would then disown a
record that matched the wrong machine rather than leaving the field empty.

### R2 THE ACTIVITY<->GAMEPLAY JOIN KEY (measured on four independent samples)
`memberKey & 0xFFFFFF == machineId >> 40`.
  p2-165  mac 0xE4BD4543DC3C74D5 <-> 0x3C74D501ECA34753     rig 0x846C8338F7D022E6 <-> 0xD022E60133B46B99
  p2-166  mac 0xE4BD4543DC3C74D5 <-> 0x3C74D501B6B1AC75     rig 0x846C8338F7D022E6 <-> 0xD022E601503B8D9E
The machine ids CHANGED between boots while the matching 24 bits stayed stable - so this
is a real derivation, not one boot's coincidence. It is a TRUNCATED key: two rows can
collide, so `net_addr_for_member` fails closed on ambiguity rather than picking one.

  - 2x `result=no_admitted_row present=0 member=0x846C...22E6` - published nothing.

kTransportIdentityFieldIndex 10 -> 11. Result:

correct index change does and what an accidental shift does not.

## 20.285 *** THE cond5 FRONT, READ END TO END (STATIC, NO BOOT): THE GATE IS A PURE DATA READ WITH NO SECOND PATH, SO ONLY THE BYTE CAN CHANGE THE OUTCOME. THE WALK SKIPS SELF (so the local player is NOT a control for it). AND THE PROBE'S "would-construct" LABEL IS WRONG: A PASSING GATE CONSTRUCTS NOTHING - IT PERFORMS THE CLAIM AS A SIDE EFFECT AND ITS RETURN FEEDS ONLY A DIAGNOSTIC STRING. THE OBJECTIVE SURVIVES; THE REASON FOR IT CHANGES. (2026-09-03, VERIFIED-BY-READING) ***

### R1 cond5 IS SIX INSTRUCTIONS AND HAS NO ALTERNATIVE PATH
0x1404dd470(rcx=table, edx=index): `al = (byte[table + index*0x2AC0 + 0x38] >> 4) & 1; ret`
No branches, no second input, no other caller of the walk's decision. Every "find another
way to reach the guard" approach is dead by construction: the ONLY thing that can change
the outcome is that byte. Combined with 20.234 (no code computes it) and 20.252/20.254
(it arrives via a wholesale image copy), the byte's origin is the whole question.

### R2 THE WALK'S FULL PRECONDITION CHAIN (0x141702630 loop, fragment of 0x141702580)
For the guard to be called for participant i, in order:
  1. `cmp ebp,r12d; je` - i must NOT be the self index (r12d from 0x1403cb2f0)
  2. `shr edx,cl; test dl,1; je` - bit i of maskA set                          (cond3)
  3. `call 0x1404df500` -> rsi = the slot base
  4. `call 0x1404df600; test al,al; jne` - next record's first byte must be 0   (cond4)
  5. `call 0x1404dd470; test al,al; jne 0x1417026f1` - the gate bit            (cond5)
CORRECTION TO THE POSTMORTEM'S FRAMING: step 1 SKIPS SELF. The local player is therefore
not "the working case failing the same gate" for THIS walk - it is never evaluated by it.
Whatever renders the local player is a different mechanism, and cannot be used as the
control here.

### R3 THE GUARD CALL'S ARGUMENTS CONFIRM 20.280 BY READING
0x141702728 calls 0x141703910 with rcx=r15, edx=ebp(index), r8b=al(0x1404df620),
r9=rsi+0x142, [rsp+0x20]=rsi+0x1ee, [rsp+0x28]=bl(0x1404df650). arg4/arg5 are exactly the
two 86-byte arrays 20.280 named. Inside, ent_gate computes edx=[[rcx+8]+8]+6 - the
container-derived bit index (the "+6" of the birth-set word) - and calls 0x1417c40f0 with
r8 = the card. This was assumed-by-reading before; it is now read.

### R4 *** THE RETURN VALUE IS DIAGNOSTIC. THE CLAIM IS A SIDE EFFECT. ***
The guard's return goes to exactly one place:
  `test al,al; movzx r13d,r13b; mov eax,0; cmove r13d,eax`  - an AND-accumulator
and r13's only consumer is at loop end:
  `test r13b,r13b; je skip` -> `0x141a8d4b0` (a one-instruction getter `mov eax,[rcx]`)
  -> compare against [r15+0x138], skip if unchanged -> `0x1404fb380` -> store the new value
0x1404fb380 (0x1404fb380..0x1404fb768) builds TWO formatted strings: a stack-built format
at [rbp-0x20], destination buffer at [rbp+0x120], two `cmovne` selections between the
one-character string pool entries "Y" (0x141BEA5C0) and "N" (0x141BC8E90), through the
varargs formatter 0x140092e50 (0x140-byte buffer -> 0x1402f90c0). It is a REPORTER.
CONSEQUENCE: passing cond5 does NOT construct an entity. Our probe's
"ALL-PASS-would-construct" verdict string was an inherited label, never verified, and it
is now corrected to "ALL-PASS-would-claim". Note also that r13 is an AND across EVERY
iterated participant - one failing peer suppresses the payoff for all of them.

### R5 THE OBJECTIVE SURVIVES - FOR A DIFFERENT REASON
Invoking the guard still matters, but for its SIDE EFFECT, not its verdict: ent_gate takes
the card into the find-or-create/claim path (0x1417c40f0 -> 0x1417cf0e0), and that claim is
what stops the admission sweep disowning the record (20.280). So "get the guard invoked"
remains the right goal; "because it would construct the peer" was the wrong reason, and
anyone reading the old verdict string would have carried that error into the next front.

0x1403CB340 (clean .pdata start), log direction (publish src=table vs restore dest=table),

watch crashed both machines and took the boot down with it. That watch is now retired at
